During the fall and spring of 2026 I had the chance to work with Professor Leocadia Paliulis, from the Biology department at Bucknell, on yet another previously completed Senior Design project.

This time, she described the situation to me as having worked well for a while, but quickly fading in usefulness. The high-power microscope she uses to study bats, spiders, and many types of biological samples has become increasingly more difficult to use. Around a decade ago, an electrical engineering student undertook the process of setting up better lights and fine motor control for Paliulis to be able to control a glass rod finely enough to pop individual molecules with precision. This system was running on a Raspberry Pi, and did work, but was becoming very slow and unreliable. She wanted an update with something a little more lightweight and usable long-term.

To that end, I decided to use an FTDI chip that would simply act as a translator between USB and SPI, to cut out a microcontroller and much of the complexity inherent in implementing one. The FTDI FT2232H series of devices are focused on an MPSSE, or Multi-Protocol Synchronous Serial Engine, which is a software-controllable form of interaction between many different types of serial communication. In addition to the FTDI chip taking care of translation, I planned to integrate a system with a large box and several power supplies into a few voltage regulators in a small footprint, allowing for switching the voltage on one port for backlights and for simultaneous outputs of multiple voltages for a fan and backlights.

This project is still in progress and will get updated soon. The current state of the board may be seen in the images. —
